question: Do the cheap sunglasses have good UV protection?
answer_text: A dark tint and UV protection are two different things, and it is entirely possible to buy sunglasses that are very dark and protect your eyes badly. The tint controls visible light; UV protection is a property of the lens material and its UV-absorbing treatment, so a deeply tinted lens with no UV treatment can suppress the light that makes you squint while passing ultraviolet through. Look for an explicit UV400 claim (blocks up to 400 nm, covering the UVA and UVB range that matters for the eye) rather than judging by darkness, and treat filter category 0-4 as a separate decision about visible light. My longer explainer: https://teenyoun.com/articles/what-uv400-actually-means-and-why-a-dark-tint-is-not-uv-protection.html

question: Are high index lenses worth it, or are they merely cosmetic?
answer_text:
Not cosmetic, but not automatically worth it either. The honest answer depends on your prescription power.

Index describes how strongly a material bends light, so for the same power a higher-index lens can be made thinner. That part is real optics, not marketing.

The cost is dispersion, and the Abbe number measures it. CR-39 sits near 1.50 with an Abbe number around 58; polycarbonate is about 1.586 with an Abbe number near 30; the 1.67 and 1.74 materials land in the low 30s as well. A lower Abbe number means more chromatic aberration, which shows up as colour fringing toward the edge of the lens and reduced contrast away from the optical centre. Higher-index surfaces also reflect more light, which is why these lenses benefit so much from a good anti-reflective coating.

Two things people usually miss. First, higher-index materials are generally denser, so a thinner lens is not automatically a lighter one. Second, the thickness you actually save scales with your prescription: at a mild power the millimetres saved are small enough that the better optical quality of a lower-index material may serve you better, while at a strong minus power the saving is the difference between a comfortable lens and a heavy one. In practice, many opticians start steering people toward higher index from roughly plus or minus 3 dioptres and up.

I wrote a longer breakdown of index, Abbe number and dispersion here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/lens-index-and-abbe-number-why-thinner-glasses-aren-t-always-better.html

question: How do you see in the dark?
answer_text:
You do not see in the dark with the same system you use in daylight. There are two, and they take turns.

The cones give you colour and fine detail, and they need reasonable light. The rods carry vision in near darkness. They contain rhodopsin, a pigment that is bleached by light and has to be rebuilt, and that rebuilding is what dark adaptation actually is. Roughly speaking, the cone system has done most of its adjusting within five to ten minutes, while full rod adaptation takes twenty to thirty minutes or more. The two-phase feel of walking into a cinema, first grey shapes and then detail, is that difference.

Two details explain most of the practical experience. First, the rod system is not simply a more sensitive copy of the cone system. Rod sensitivity peaks at around 507 nanometres, in the blue-green, while cone sensitivity peaks nearer 555 nanometres, which is why colour drains towards grey in dim light. Second, adaptation is partly mechanical: the pupil opens in darkness and admits more light, and that part reverses quickly.

Because of this, a bright light resets much of the work, since a single exposure bleaches a meaningful amount of rhodopsin. It is also why yellow night-driving lenses do not help. They cut the blue-green wavelengths the rod system is most sensitive to, removing light exactly where your eye is using it.

If your dark adaptation has become noticeably slower than it used to be, that is worth having assessed rather than accepted.

I wrote about what does and does not help night vision here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/night-driving-glasses-do-yellow-lenses-actually-help-.html

question: Eyewear: What is the minimum lens height for progressive bifocals?
answer_text:
You are looking for one number, and the honest answer is that the number belongs to the lens design rather than to progressive lenses in general.

A progressive lens is one surface whose power changes gradually down a corridor. The distance zone sits at the top, the reading zone at the bottom, and the corridor connects them. Every design therefore has a published minimum fitting height, measured from the fitting cross at the pupil down to the point where the reading zone becomes usable. Minimums commonly cited fall in the 18 to 22 mm range, and frames are usually recommended to have roughly 30 mm of vertical depth to carry a progressive comfortably. Those figures are the ones you will see quoted repeatedly; the exact number for your pair is on the design's technical sheet.

The reason a minimum exists at all is geometric. The fitting cross is placed at the pupil, and everything the lens can do sits below it. If the usable depth below the pupil is shorter than the corridor plus the reading zone, the reading zone is cut off by the frame rim. Nothing is wrong with the lens; there was not enough glass where the reading area needed to be. What the wearer notices is that reading requires dropping the chin or tilting the head, because the only comfortable near zone now sits at the very bottom edge.

Two distinctions are worth keeping separate. Fitting height is where your pupil sits relative to the frame, measured on your face in a natural posture; it is not the frame's total height. And a progressive is not a lined bifocal: there is no segment to measure, so the relevant value is the design's minimum rather than a segment height.

If someone quotes you a minimum without asking for your measured fitting height and the design being sold, that number was not about you.

I wrote about what fitting height actually determines here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/multifocal-fitting-height-why-the-reading-zone-has-to-match-your-gaze.html

question: Why does everything look so small through my eye glasses?
answer_text:
Because a spectacle lens does not just bend light to a focus. It also scales the image, and for a short-sighted prescription the scaling is downward.
The useful way to think about it is the power factor of spectacle magnification. It is written as 1 / (1 - dF), where d is the distance from the back of the lens to your eye in metres and F is the lens power in dioptres.
Take a -5.00 D lens sitting 14 mm in front of the eye, so d = 0.014. The denominator becomes 1 - (0.014 x -5.00) = 1 + 0.07 = 1.07, and the factor is about 0.935. Everything you see through that lens arrives roughly 6.5 per cent smaller than it would with no lens in the way. Push the same lens further from the eye and d grows and the image shrinks further, with no change to the prescription at all.
Two consequences follow that surprise people.
The first is why contact lenses change how the world looks. A contact lens sits essentially on the eye, so d is close to zero and the minification largely disappears. Somebody who has worn -5.00 glasses for years and switches to contacts does not just see more clearly; the world gets bigger, and doorways, stairs and the distance between the car and the kerb all need a few days of recalibration.
The second is that a plus prescription does the opposite. For a positive F the denominator drops below 1 and the factor rises above 1, so a long-sighted prescription enlarges rather than shrinks.
There is a second contributor, sometimes called the shape factor, which comes from the curvature of the lens itself rather than its distance from the eye, and in real glasses the two are multiplied together. That is why two people with the same power can still disagree about how much smaller things look: their lenses differ in thickness and base curve.
If your two eyes need very different powers, the images also differ in size from each other, which is a separate problem the visual system has to fuse.
I wrote about this in more detail, including the shape factor, here:
https://teenyoun.com/articles/why-your-glasses-change-the-size-of-the-world-spectacle-magnification-explained.html

question: Why can’t I see my phone screen when using polarized sunglasses?
answer_text:
The short answer is that your phone screen is already a polarising filter, and your sunglasses are a second one sitting in front of it.

A liquid crystal display works by putting a liquid crystal layer between two polarising filters. Voltage twists the crystals, which controls how much of the backlight gets past the second filter. The light that leaves the screen is therefore not a jumble of vibration directions at all. It is polarised along one axis, set by the panel's construction.

Your sunglasses do the same job in reverse. A polarising lens passes light vibrating along one direction and absorbs the rest, and in sunglasses that axis is normally vertical, so that it rejects the horizontal glare bouncing off water, roads and car bodies.

Put the two together and you have a pair of crossed polarisers. What happens next follows Malus's law: the fraction of light transmitted equals the square of the cosine of the angle between the two axes. Aligned, cos²0° = 1 and everything passes. At 45 degrees, cos²45° = 0.5, so half the light gets through. At 90 degrees, cos²90° = 0, and in principle nothing passes at all.

That is why the screen does not simply look dim. It looks black in one orientation and normal in another. Turn the phone a quarter turn, or tilt your head ninety degrees, and you have moved from crossed polarisers to aligned ones. The phone is not faulty and neither are the lenses.

Two details explain why your experience may differ from someone else's. Not every display leaves its light linearly polarised in the same way. Screens that carry a circular polariser on the front, which is common on phones where the layer is there to control reflections, change the light to circularly polarised instead. A linear filter in front of that dims the screen whatever the angle, so it looks grey rather than black, and rotating it does nothing. The axis is also fixed relative to the device, so a phone that polarises vertically in portrait can behave completely differently in landscape.

If it bothers you, rotating the device is the free fix. If you rely on a heads-up display or read a digital dashboard, mention it when choosing glasses: tint and polarisation are separate choices, and it is far easier to specify before the lenses are made.

I wrote about the physics of polarised lenses and reflected light here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/how-polarized-lenses-cut-glare-the-physics-of-reflected-light.html

question: Why do my eyes feel tired after staring at a screen all day?
answer_text:
Screen fatigue is usually described as if one part of the eye wears out. In practice it is three reflexes pulling on each other at once, plus a tear film that quietly stops being replenished. Understanding the linkage explains why the usual fixes work when they work, and why others do nothing.

Focusing at near is active work, not a resting state. To focus closer than infinity the ciliary muscle contracts, which slackens the zonular fibres and lets the crystalline lens take up a rounder, higher-powered shape. That is a muscle holding a posture for as long as you keep looking at the screen. The capacity is finite and declines with age, which is why the same screen distance that was effortless at 25 becomes work at 45.

The eyes must also turn inward, in a fixed ratio to the focusing. Convergence demand is set by distance and by your pupillary distance. At 60 cm with a 60 mm PD the demand is about 10 prism dioptres; at 30 cm it doubles to about 20. The ratio linking the two systems — convergence per dioptre of accommodation — is normally around 4 to 6 prism dioptres per dioptre. Because they share control signals, an error in one shows up as a symptom in the other.

The pupils constrict as well, which buys depth of field at the cost of light. Smaller pupils sharpen a slightly defocused image, which is why screen work in a bright room can feel easier than the same work at night — and why squinting helps for a moment: you are stopping the system down.

Sustained accommodation and convergence are part of the discomfort, but blinking is the missing variable in most discussions. Concentrated screen work suppresses blink rate and changes blink completeness, so the tear film breaks up between blinks and the optical surface itself becomes irregular. That is why symptoms often respond to a humidifier, a conscious blink habit or lubricating drops, and only partly to a new prescription.

Three claims I would push back on. First, "blue light is why your eyes hurt": filtering short wavelengths does not address a muscular posture or a tear film, and the discomfort tracks the task rather than the spectrum. Second, "20-20-20 works because it exercises the eye": it works mainly because it releases accommodation, restores blinking and lets the tear film recover; nothing is being strengthened. Third, "if the prescription is right, screen fatigue is not an eye problem": a correct prescription at the wrong working distance still leaves a large accommodative demand, and working distance is part of the prescription decision.

See an optometrist if the fatigue is one-sided, if you see double at near, if you keep pushing material further away, if headaches cluster after reading but not after other tasks, or if symptoms persist after a refraction. Amplitude, accommodative response, facility and binocular posture are all measurable, and they answer a different question from "what is my prescription".

I wrote a longer explanation of how the three responses are wired together, including the AC/A ratio, here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/the-near-triad-why-focusing-converging-and-pupil-size-move-together.html

question: Why do my new glasses make things look curved?
answer_text:
Curved doorframes and a floor that seems to tilt are usually not a mistake in your prescription. They are the signature of a lens doing something it has always done, seen for the first time because the numbers changed.
Four mechanisms produce the effect.
Distortion. A powered lens does not magnify the same amount everywhere: magnification changes with distance from the optical centre. Minus lenses bend straight lines outward at the edge, plus lenses bend them inward. The further from the centre you look, and the stronger the power, the more pronounced it is.
Meridional magnification. If you have astigmatism, the two principal meridians carry different powers and therefore magnify differently. A square can come out slightly wider than it is tall, which is why some people describe a squashed or stretched world rather than a curved one.
Prismatic effect. Prentice's rule is P = c × F: the prism at a point equals the distance from the optical centre in centimetres multiplied by the power in dioptres. Eight millimetres off centre at -6.00 D works out to 4.8 prism dioptres. That displaces the image, and it displaces it by different amounts in the two eyes, so the world appears to swing when you move your gaze.
Base curve and wrap. A different front curve changes both the magnification and the oblique aberrations, and a wrapped frame contributes prism of its own before any prescription is ground.
Why it usually fades. The visual system recalibrates the mapping between retinal image and perceived space. Most people settle within days to two weeks, and the process is faster when the change in power is small and the optical centres are well placed.
What is not normal. Distortion in one eye only, distortion that appears on a pair you have worn comfortably for months, effects that are still there after four weeks, or distortion accompanied by double vision. Those point to measurement, lens position or a lens that has been stressed in its frame rather than to adaptation.
One clarification about warped lenses. A thin or rimless lens can be distorted by mounting stress, and that is worth checking. But if the bowing is symmetrical, affects both eyes equally and appears only with the new pair, it is design and geometry doing their normal work rather than damage.
I wrote a longer explanation of the four mechanisms, including when the effect should be investigated, here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/straight-lines-that-bend-why-new-glasses-make-the-world-curve.html

question: Why do things look smaller in one eye?
answer_text:
Two eyes can report different image sizes for two quite different reasons, and separating them decides what can actually be done.
The first is optical and arithmetic. If the two eyes need very different corrections, the spectacles themselves magnify by different amounts. A minus lens minifies, a plus lens magnifies, and the amount depends on power and on how far the lens sits from the eye. The power factor is 1 divided by (1 minus d times F), where d is the vertex distance in metres and F the power. Take a -6.00 D lens sitting 12 mm from the eye: 0.012 times -6 is -0.072, so the factor is 1 divided by 1.072, about 0.93. That eye's image is roughly 7 per cent smaller than it would be with no lens at all. The other eye, if it is plano or only slightly corrected, gets almost no minification. The difference between the two eyes is the problem, not the absolute size.
The second is retinal. Even with identical corrections, the two eyes can produce different-sized images because of differences in the optical system behind the lens, or in the density of retinal receptors. This is aniseikonia proper, and it cannot be fixed by changing the glasses prescription.
The threshold matters. A difference of one or two per cent is usually tolerated without complaint. Somewhere around four to five per cent, most people start to notice distortion, a pulling sensation when reading, headache, or an inability to fuse the two images comfortably. Above that, symptoms are the rule rather than the exception.
What helps depends on which mechanism is at work. Shortening the vertex distance reduces the magnification difference. Contact lenses remove vertex distance from the equation almost entirely, which is why a highly anisometropic person may do better in contacts than in glasses. Careful frame selection, iseikonic lens designs, and deliberate under-correction of the more affected eye are all strategies an optometrist can weigh.
Two things deserve prompt attention rather than an online answer. A size difference that appeared suddenly, especially in one eye, or one accompanied by distortion of straight lines, a central shadow, or recent trauma, is not a spectacle problem and needs an examination quickly. And a persistent difference that has never been assessed is worth measuring properly, because the size of the difference can be quantified rather than guessed at.
I wrote the fuller explanation, including the shape factor and how the threshold is measured, here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/aniseikonia-when-the-two-eyes-see-different-sizes.html

question: Why do things look distorted with glasses that are -15.50 and -13.50? I wear contacts and got glasses in case of emergency but the doors look bowed and the ground seems like it is slanted. It's hard to even walk in them.
Where is my pupillary distance on my prescription?
answer_text:
Your eye doctor often does not record it because a prescription describes what your eyes need, while PD describes where the lenses have to sit. That second number belongs to whoever is making the glasses, so it is frequently absent from the printout you are handed, and yes, you generally have to ask for it explicitly.

Ask the optician rather than the doctor. The useful phrasing is "I need my PD, including monocular PD, for an online order." Most will give it. Some charge a small fee or decline to release it, which is a policy choice, not a legal restriction. Monocular PD, one number per eye, is better than a single binocular value because faces are rarely symmetrical.

You can also measure it yourself, accurately enough for ordinary single-vision orders. Stand about 20 cm from a mirror, hold a millimetre ruler flat against your brow with the zero mark over one pupil, keep your head still, close that eye, and read the mark that lines up with the centre of the other pupil. Do it twice. If the two readings differ by more than a millimetre, take a third and use that one. Most adults land between about 58 and 70 mm, so a result far outside that range usually means the ruler was read from the wrong mark.

Why the precision matters: each lens has an optical centre that should sit directly in front of the pupil it serves. A few millimetres off and you are looking through the edge of the lens, where prism and aberration live. The symptom is rarely obvious blur. It shows up as eye strain, a pulling ache above the eyes, or a headache that arrives after twenty minutes of reading, which is exactly why a wrong PD goes unnoticed for months.

One caveat on DIY. A ruler measurement is fine for a low-power single-vision pair. If you wear a high prescription, prism, or a progressive, the tolerance is much tighter and the professional measurement is worth the fee.

The full method, including the two-person check and the dual-PD case: https://teenyoun.com/articles/how-to-measure-pupillary-distance-at-home-3-easy-methods.html
